turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have no interest in being deceived by your attempts to whitewash Wickham's character, Mr. Darcy. You have had ample opportunity to defend yourself, and yet you have chosen to remain silent on the matter.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, Miss Bennet, that you would refuse my offer based on such frivolous and unfounded grievances. My behavior towards Wickham, though misguided, was motivated by a desire to protect your sister from his dishonorable intentions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I suppose you think it's amusing to parade your supposed gallantry in front of me, Mr. Darcy, after having treated me with such disdain in the past.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I find your refusal of my offer to be a grave disappointment, not only for myself, but for the prospect of a union that could have elevated your family's standing in society.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must admit, Mr. Darcy, that I am shocked by your audacity in suggesting that my refusal of your offer is a disappointment to you, when you have shown me nothing but disdain and disrespect in the past.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you reconsider your decision, Miss Bennet, for I am convinced that a union between us would be advantageous to both your family and mine.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not so desperate for a good marriage as to settle for a union with someone who has consistently shown me that he values pride and privilege over honesty and decency.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must remind you, Miss Bennet, that a union between us is not merely a matter of personal preference, but a pragmatic arrangement that would be beneficial to both our families.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: How dare you, Mr. Darcy, speak of our union as a pragmatic arrangement, when you have so consistently shown yourself to be a man of pride and arrogance, caring little for the well-being of others, including my own family.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I find your rejection of my offer to be not only unwise, but also a testament to your own lack of judgment and discernment.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not interested in your condescending lectures on my judgment, Mr. Darcy. I know exactly what I am doing, and it is not settling for a life with someone who has made it clear they value my family's connections over my own feelings and well-being.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I see no reason to continue this conversation, Mr. Darcy, as it is clear we are not suited for marriage or any sort of close relationship, given your continued lack of understanding and respect for me and my family.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you reconsider your decision, Miss Bennet, as I firmly believe that our union would be beneficial to both of us, despite your reservations.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You have no idea what is beneficial to me, Mr. Darcy, and it is laughable that you think you do.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must say, Miss Bennet, that your persistent refusal to consider my proposal is a mystery to me. I have done everything in my power to demonstrate my suitability as a husband, and yet you continue to reject me. I fear that your feelings towards me are inextricably tied to your family's disapproval, and that you are allowing their prejudices to guide your judgment.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not being swayed by your attempts to shift the blame, Mr. Darcy. You have consistently shown a lack of respect for me and my family, and I will not be persuaded to overlook that.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I find it quite vexing to be rejected by a young woman who, in my opinion, is not yet in a position to make an informed decision about her future.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You would not know an informed decision if it bit you, Mr. Darcy. I have had ample opportunity to observe your behavior, and I will not be swayed by empty professions of love.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that my proposals are not driven by a desire to alleviate your family's financial struggles, nor am I attempting to secure a advantageous alliance through marriage. My interest in you, Miss Bennet, is genuine, and I will not be deterred by your continued rejection.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be convinced by your words, Mr. Darcy, when your actions have shown me time and again that you value your own pride and prejudices above the welfare of others.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
